question_facts.name: 零冠词与固定冠词用法
question_facts.question_body: It's time for meeting. Tom went up the stairs so fast—two at ______ time, but he was still late.
question_facts.question_text: It's time for meeting. Tom went up the stairs so fast—two at ______ time, but he was still late.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查固定搭配。at a time 是固定短语，意为“一次，每次”。two at a time 意为“一次迈两个（台阶）”。句意为：汤姆上楼很快，一次迈两个台阶，但他还是迟到了。

question_facts.name: many/much/few/little等数量限定词
question_facts.question_body: Mike is good at English, but sometimes he still has ______ problems.
question_facts.question_text: Mike is good at English, but sometimes he still has ______ problems.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查数量形容词。problems 是可数名词复数，排除修饰不可数名词的 A 和 B。few 表示“几乎没有”（否定），a few 表示“有一些”（肯定）。根据 but 的转折关系，迈克英语很好，但“仍然有一些”问题，故选 C。

question_facts.name: some/any/no/every及复合不定代词
question_facts.question_body: Oh, Maggie, I have ______ to tell you about my trip to France.
question_facts.question_text: Oh, Maggie, I have ______ to tell you about my trip to France.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查不定代词与形容词的位置及用法。当形容词修饰不定代词（如 something, anything 等）时，形容词需后置，排除 A 和 D。something 用于肯定句，anything 用于否定句或疑问句。本句是肯定句，表示“有一些有趣的事要告诉你”，故选 B。

question_facts.name: 形容词、副词的句法位置与修饰功能
question_facts.question_body: The old woman can't see the message on the mobile phone ______.
question_facts.question_text: The old woman can't see the message on the mobile phone ______.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查副词修饰动词及 enough 的位置。修饰动词 see 应使用副词 clearly；enough 修饰副词或形容词时需放在其后。因此应为 clearly enough，意为“足够清楚地”。

question_facts.question_text: The 2025 Mid-Autumn Festival gala brought the audience an audiovisual feast ______ Monday night.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查时间介词。在具体的某个晚上的表达中，通常使用介词 on。on Monday night 指“在周一晚上”。

question_facts.name: 并列连词与关联连词
question_facts.question_body: ______ Kate ______ her cousin has been to Russia, but both of them have known the country very well.
question_facts.question_text: ______ Kate ______ her cousin has been to Russia, but both of them have known the country very well.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查并列连词及语境逻辑。根据后半句 but 引导的转折“但他们两人对这个国家都很了解”可推知，前半句应是“凯特和她的表兄都没去过俄罗斯”。Neither... nor... 意为“既不……也不……”，且谓语动词 has 符合就近原则。

question_facts.name: 从属连词的语义关系
question_facts.question_body: Michael wasn't late for work this morning ______ he missed the early bus.
question_facts.question_text: Michael wasn't late for work this morning ______ he missed the early bus.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查连词辨析。句意为：迈克尔今天早上上班没有迟到，______他错过了早班车。上下文存在让步关系，即“尽管”错过了车，但没迟到，故选 though。

question_facts.name: 比较结构与比较范围
question_facts.question_body:
- This song seems ______ these days. It was played everywhere when it came out.
- That's true. We seldom hear it now.
question_facts.question_text:
- This song seems ______ these days. It was played everywhere when it came out.
- That's true. We seldom hear it now.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查形容词比较等级。根据下文“We seldom hear it now（我们现在很少听到了）”以及“these days”与刚出来时到处播放的对比，可知这首歌现在“不那么流行了”，故用 less popular。

question_facts.name: 一般时态的被动语态
question_facts.question_body: Paper decorations for the art festival ______ from the ceiling in every classroom last month.
question_facts.question_text: Paper decorations for the art festival ______ from the ceiling in every classroom last month.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查动词时态、语态及辨析。last month 表示过去，需用一般过去时。decoraions 与 hang（悬挂）是被动关系，需用被动语态（was/were + 过去分词）。hang 表示“悬挂”时过去分词为 hung（hanged 意为“处以绞刑”），故选 B。

question_facts.name: 感叹句what/how结构
question_facts.question_body: ______ important information Miss Green told us!
question_facts.question_text: ______ important information Miss Green told us!
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查感叹句。information 是不可数名词。感叹不可数名词的结构为：What + 形容词 + 不可数名词 + 主语 + 谓语！故选 B。

question_facts.question_body: The young man is good at ______ traditional Chinese cutting.
question_facts.question_text: The young man is good at ______ traditional Chinese cutting.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查固定搭配。be good at doing sth. 意为“擅长做某事”，at 是介词，后面接动词的 -ing 形式，故选 making。

question_facts.name: 情态动词推测、否定与简略回答
question_facts.question_body:
- Listen! Is that Bill singing in the next room?
- No, it ______ be Bill. He has gone to the playground.
question_facts.question_text:
- Listen! Is that Bill singing in the next room?
- No, it ______ be Bill. He has gone to the playground.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查情态动词表示推测。根据“He has gone to the playground”可知，他不在房间里，所以“不可能是”比尔。can't 表示有把握的否定推测，故选 A。

question_facts.name: 时间、条件状语从句及主将从现
question_facts.question_body: Peter doesn't tell me when he ______. I'll telephone you as soon as he ______.
question_facts.question_text: Peter doesn't tell me when he ______. I'll telephone you as soon as he ______.
question_facts.ai_solution_process: 本题考查时态用法。第一句 when 引导宾语从句，根据语境应用将来时 will come；第二句 as soon as 引导时间状语从句，遵循“主将从现”原则，从句应用一般现在时表示将来，主语 he 为单三，故用 comes。

question_facts.question_text: Tom fell off the bike and hurt his leg yesterday. ______, he had to be away from school for two or three months.

question_facts.question_text:

Many years has passed, Ma Li is still sticking to her work. Every day she gets up early and works hard. She sees at least 10 patients, sometimes even 30 or 40. It may be many {{39}} walk to a patient's home.

Discovering the Power of Placebos (安慰剂)
A little girl cries after falling and bumping her knee against the ground. Her father rushes over and looks closely at the leg. “I'll kiss it and make it better,” he says. The kiss works. The girl sniffles (抽噎), then jumps up and gets back to playing. Her pain is {{65}}.
Things like this one happen on playgrounds and in homes around the world every day. When a child gets a bump or bruise (淤伤), says Ulrike Bingel, “Someone will blow the pain away.” Bingel is a doctor at a Germany university.
A caring adult seems to have the ability to stop a child's pain with a puff of air, a kiss or even just a few kind words. {{66}}, none of these things can repair injured skin. So what's happening? Doctors call it the placebo effect. It describes what happens when something that should have no effect leads to a(n) {{67}} positive change in someone's body.
Placebos are a very {{68}} part of medical research. To prove that a new medicine works, researchers must show that the people who are taking a new drug will be in much better health than those who are taking a placebo. This placebo is usually a pill and it {{69}} the same as the new medicine but contains no medicine. At times a person may feel better after taking a placebo pill though the pill did not act on any disease.
This placebo response isn't an illusion (幻觉). It comes from the brain. A placebo effect can only influence body processes that the brain can change like a pain. “Placebos can't fight cancer,” Bingel says, “But they can change how {{70}} someone experiences pain or other illness.” Bingel and his team are working to better understand what brain processes make this happen.

Some people will use AI to do something harmful to people on the Internet. We should be careful when we are surfing on the Internet. Thank you very much.

strengths: Addresses all parts of the prompt (two changes + one viewpoint).
weaknesses: Overuse of the definite article 'the' with abstract/uncountable nouns.
suggestions: Practice using abstract nouns without 'the' when speaking in general terms.

As a young piano player and a 7th-grader, Toby has always been curious about the effects of music on people. He has done many tests on this. When he learned that people find it hard to focus, he wondered, “Could music help us improve attention?”

He then started an online test. He asked 65 people to play a computer game — they had to press a key when they saw certain numbers. Those people were divided into three groups. During the game, one group played in silence. Another group listened to a song from a video game. The third group heard a different tone (音调) in each ear, which created a special beating sound.
After the test, Toby compared the results. He found that the group with the special two-tone sound did the best. The group with the video game music did the worst. Although the results weren’t strong enough to be completely sure, Toby didn’t see that as a failure. For him, it was a starting point for more learning. “If you try something and it doesn’t work, that’s not a problem,” he said. “It’s part of the study process.”
Later, Toby’s project won him a prize in a national science contest. He hopes his work will help students discover new ways to focus when they study.

question_facts.material_text:
Vicky, a 14-year-old schoolgirl, was having difficulty with a piece of writing in English. She thought hard but achieved nothing, so she asked her teacher for some ideas to get started. In the end, she wrote one of her best pieces of work. She was really pleased that she had asked for help.
Everyone finds things difficult sometimes — Vicky is not the only one. Learning how to ask others to lend a hand is an important life skill.
When you might need help: There are lots of reasons why you could need help, such as having trouble with schoolwork or learning a new skill. When you’re finding something difficult, or it’s taking a long time to make progress, asking for help will move you forward more quickly than {{57}}.
What stops you asking for help: Asking for help isn’t always easy. It can be tricky if you’re not sure who to ask because you might think they won’t want to help or they haven’t got the time. If you think asking for a helping hand is a sign of weakness, it makes it even harder to turn to another person.
Asking for support is brave: Asking for help is an act of bravery. It takes great courage to let someone in, trust them with your story and ask them to help you deal with a problem.
When you ask for help, you won’t face the pressure alone. As an old saying goes, “A problem shared is a problem halved.” There are other benefits too. By asking for help, you learn to express what you need. You can also put yourself in others’ shoes and be more able to offer a helping hand when someone needs it.

question_fact.material_text:
Discovering the Power of Placebos (安慰剂)
A little girl cries after falling and bumping her knee against the ground. Her father rushes over and looks closely at the leg. “I'll kiss it and make it better,” he says. The kiss works. The girl sniffles (抽噎), then jumps up and gets back to playing. Her pain is {{65}}.
Things like this one happen on playgrounds and in homes around the world every day. When a child gets a bump or bruise (淤伤), says Ulrike Bingel, “Someone will blow the pain away.” Bingel is a doctor at a Germany university.
A caring adult seems to have the ability to stop a child's pain with a puff of air, a kiss or even just a few kind words. {{66}}, none of these things can repair injured skin. So what's happening? Doctors call it the placebo effect. It describes what happens when something that should have no effect leads to a(n) {{67}} positive change in someone's body.
Placebos are a very {{68}} part of medical research. To prove that a new medicine works, researchers must show that the people who are taking a new drug will be in much better health than those who are taking a placebo. This placebo is usually a pill and it {{69}} the same as the new medicine but contains no medicine. At times a person may feel better after taking a placebo pill though the pill did not act on any disease.
This placebo response isn't an illusion (幻觉). It comes from the brain. A placebo effect can only influence body processes that the brain can change like a pain. “Placebos can't fight cancer,” Bingel says, “But they can change how {{70}} someone experiences pain or other illness.” Bingel and his team are working to better understand what brain processes make this happen.

As a young piano player and a 7th-grader, Toby has always been curious about the effects of music on people. He has done many tests on this. When he learned that people find it hard to focus, he wondered, “Could music help us improve attention?”
This 14-year-old boy started to search online for the effects of different kinds of music. He wanted to find out if listening to certain kinds of sounds could make people more focused. He then started an online test. He asked 65 people to play a computer game — they had to press a key when they saw certain numbers. Those people were divided into three groups. During the game, one group played in silence. Another group listened to a song from a video game. The third group heard a different tone (音调) in each ear, which created a special beating sound.
After the test, Toby compared the results. He found that the group with the special two-tone sound did the best. The group with the video game music did the worst. Although the results weren’t strong enough to be completely sure, Toby didn’t see that as a failure. For him, it was a starting point for more learning. “If you try something and it doesn’t work, that’s not a problem,” he said. “It’s part of the study process.”
Later, Toby’s project won him a prize in a national science contest. He hopes his work will help students discover new ways to focus when they study.

question_fact.material_text:
Vicky, a 14-year-old schoolgirl, was having difficulty with a piece of writing in English. She thought hard but achieved nothing, so she asked her teacher for some ideas to get started. In the end, she wrote one of her best pieces of work. She was really pleased that she had asked for help.
Everyone finds things difficult sometimes — Vicky is not the only one. Learning how to ask others to lend a hand is an important life skill.
When you might need help: There are lots of reasons why you could need help, such as having trouble with schoolwork or learning a new skill. When you’re finding something difficult, or it’s taking a long time to make progress, asking for help will move you forward more quickly than {{57}}.
What stops you asking for help: Asking for help isn’t always easy. It can be tricky if you’re not sure who to ask because you might think they won’t want to help or they haven’t got the time. If you think asking for a helping hand is a sign of weakness, it makes it even harder to turn to another person.
Asking for support is brave: Asking for help is an act of bravery. It takes great courage to let someone in, trust them with your story and ask them to help you deal with a problem.
When you ask for help, you won’t face the pressure alone. As an old saying goes, “A problem shared is a problem halved.” There are other benefits too. By asking for help, you learn to express what you need. You can also put yourself in others’ shoes and be more able to offer a helping hand when someone needs it.
